The '''Airbus A220''' is a family of five-abreast [[narrow-body airliner]]s by [[Airbus Canada Limited Partnership]] (ACLP). It was initially developed by [[Bombardier Aviation]] with the program launched on 13 July 2008 and had two years in-service as the '''Bombardier CSeries'''.
<!--1.a Development: Program launch - Certification - Entry into service-->
The smaller A220-100 (formerly CS100) [[Maiden flight|first flew]] on 16 September 2013, received an initial [[type certificate]] from [[Transport Canada]] on 18 December 2015, and entered service on 15 July 2016 with [[Swiss International Air Lines]]. The longer A220-300 (formerly CS300) first flew on 27 February 2015, received an initial type certificate on 11 July 2016, and entered service with [[airBaltic]] on 14 December 2016. Both launch operators recorded better-than-expected fuel burn and dispatch reliability, as well as positive feedback from passengers and crew.

<!--1.b Development: Production - A220 rebranding (Airbus programme acquisition + Bombardier exit participation)-->
The rebranding to A220 took place in July 2018, after [[Airbus]] acquired a majority stake in the programme through a [[joint venture]], which was subsequently renamed ACLP in June 2019. The A220 thus became the only Airbus commercial aircraft programme managed outside of Europe. In August, a second A220 final assembly line opened at the [[Airbus Mobile]] facility in [[Alabama]], supplementing the main facility in [[Mirabel, Quebec]]. In February 2020, Airbus increased its stake in ACLP to 75% through Bombardier's exit, while [[Investissement Québec]] held the remaining stake.

<!--2. Design - Variants-->
Powered by [[Pratt & Whitney PW1000G|Pratt & Whitney PW1500G]] geared turbofan engines under its wings, the [[twinjet]] features [[fly-by-wire]] flight controls, a [[carbon composite]] wing, an [[aluminium-lithium]] fuselage, and optimised aerodynamics for better [[Fuel economy in aircraft|fuel efficiency]]. The aircraft family offers [[maximum take-off weight]]s from {{cvt|63.1 to 70.9|t|lb}}, and cover a {{cvt|3450|-|3600|nmi}} [[Range (aircraft)|range]]. The 35 m (115 ft) long A220-100 seats 108 to 133, while the 38.7 m (127 ft) long A220-300 seats 130 to 160.
The ACJ TwoTwenty is the [[Airbus Corporate Jets|business jet version]] of the A220-100, launched in late 2020.

<!--3. Operators - Operational history - Orders & Deliveries-->
[[Delta Air Lines]] is the largest A220 operator with 96 aircraft in its fleet, while [[AirAsia]] is the largest customer with a total order of 150 aircraft {{As of|2026|10|lc=y}}. A total of 1,105 A220 family aircraft have been ordered of which 559 units have been delivered and 555 units are in service with 25 operators. The global A220 fleet has completed more than 2.41{{nbsp}}million flights over 4.25{{nbsp}}million block hours, transporting more than 240{{nbsp}}million passengers to 540 destinations, with one smoke-related accident. The A220 family complements the [[A319neo]] in the Airbus range and competes with [[Boeing 737 MAX|Boeing 737 MAX 7]], as well as the smaller four-abreast [[Embraer E195-E2]] and [[Embraer E190-E2|E190-E2]], with the A220 holding over 55% market share in this small airliner category.

==Development==
===BRJ-X forerunner concept===
[[File:Bombardier BRJ-X.jpg|thumb|left|''BRJ-X'', a four-abreast forerunner concept in early 1996]]

Bombardier began discussions with [[Fokker]] on 5 February 1996 about acquiring that company's assets, including the 100-seat [[Fokker 100]] short-haul aircraft.<ref>{{cite web |title=Fokker 100 Leaflet |url=http://www.flyfokker.com/downloads/FlyFokker/Leaflet%20Fokker%20100.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091127210225/http://www.flyfokker.com/downloads/FlyFokker/Leaflet%20Fokker%20100.pdf |archive-date=2009-11-27 |publisher=Fokker Services}}</ref> However, after evaluating the potential purchase, Bombardier announced an end to the talks on 27 February,<ref>{{cite press release |url= http://www.thefreelibrary.com/Bombardier+Ends+Talks+With+Fokker.-a018029019 |title= Bombardier Ends Talks With Fokker |publisher= Bombardier |date= 27 February 1996 |access-date= 29 June 2016 |archive-date= 3 April 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20190403203552/https://www.thefreelibrary.com/Bombardier+Ends+Talks+With+Fokker.-a018029019 |url-status= live}}</ref> and two weeks later, on 15 March, Fokker was declared bankrupt.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/fokker-bankrupt/10085.article |title= Fokker bankrupt |author-first1= Kevin |author-last1=O'Toole |work= Flightglobal |date= 20 March 1996 |access-date= 18 February 2022}}</ref> Bombardier then launched the ''BRJ-X'', or "Bombardier Regional Jet eXpansion" on 8 September, a larger regional jet than the ''[[Bombardier CRJ|CRJ Series]]'' or "Canadair Regional Jet" due to enter service in 2003. Instead of 2–2 seating, the BRJ-X was to have a wider [[fuselage]] with 2–3 seating for 85 to 110 passengers, and underwing [[nacelle|engine pods]].<ref name="MontrealGazetteTimeline" /> It was comparable to the smallest [[Airliner#Narrow-body airliners|narrow-body jetliners]], like the 2–3 [[DC-9]]/[[MD-80]]/[[Boeing 717]] or the 3–3 [[Airbus A318]] and [[Boeing 737-500]]/[[Boeing 737-600|737-600]]. At the end of 2000, the project was shelved by Bombardier in favour of stretching the [[Bombardier CRJ700#CRJ700|CRJ700]] into the [[Bombardier CRJ700#CRJ900|CRJ900]].<ref>{{cite news|last1=Lewis|first1=Paul|title=Bombardier puts BRJ-X on hold|url=https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/bombardier-puts-brj-x-on-hold-120369/|access-date=29 June 2016|publisher=[[Flightglobal]]|date=19 September 2000|location=Washington DC|archive-date=17 August 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160817011329/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/bombardier-puts-brj-x-on-hold-120369/|url-status=live}}</ref>

Meanwhile, [[Embraer]] launched its four-abreast [[Embraer E-Jet family|E-Jet family]] for 70 to 122 passengers in June 1999, which entered service in 2004. Airbus launched its 107–117 passengers [[Airbus A318|A318]] on 21 April 1999,<ref name=MontrealGazetteTimeline>{{cite web |url= https://montrealgazette.com/business/interactives/cseries/timeline.html |title= The CSeries: a timeline |publisher= Montreal Gazette |access-date= 27 January 2019 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20181017002048/http://www.montrealgazette.com/business/interactives/cseries/timeline.html |archive-date= 17 October 2018}}</ref> which entered service in July 2003,<ref name="Gunston">{{Cite book|last=Gunston|first=Bill|author-link=Bill Gunston|title=Airbus: The Complete Story|year=2009|location=Sparkford, Yeovil, Somerset, UK |publisher=Haynes Publishing|isbn=978-1-84425-585-6|pages=213–216, 222–223}}</ref> as Boeing had the [[737-600]] first delivered in September 1998.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/putting-the-family-to-work-51106/ |title= Putting the family to work |date= 12 May 1999 |magazine= Flight International |author-first1= Andrew |author-last1=Doyle|author-first2= Max |author-last2=Kingsley-Jones|author-first3= Paul |author-last3=Lewis|author-first4= Guy |author-last4=Norris |access-date= June 11, 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180612145307/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/putting-the-family-to-work-51106/ |archive-date= June 12, 2018 |url-status= live}}</ref>

=== Search for engines and one-year development break ===
[[File:Bombardier CS100 (26889780191).jpg|thumb|[[Pratt & Whitney|P&W]]’s new [[Geared Turbofan|GTF]] engine was selected in late 2007 to power the CSeries; it was later designated the [[Pratt & Whitney PW1000G|PW1500G]].]]

Despite government support, Bombardier had difficulty finding the right [[Propulsion|powerplant]] for the CSeries in June 2005 after failing to get the two engine consortia [[International Aero Engines]] and [[CFM International]] to compete for the CSeries contract.<ref>{{Cite news |date=6 June 2005 |title=Bombardier Still Looking for Right Engine for C-Series Airliner Family |work=Aviation Week |url=https://aviationweek.com/bombardier-still-looking-right-engine-c-series-airliner-family |access-date=14 July 2023}}</ref><ref name="FlightGlobalMay2005">{{Cite news |date=17 May 2005 |title=CSeries wins aid as engine makers quit |work=Flight Global |url=https://www.flightglobal.com/cseries-wins-aid-as-engine-makers-quit/60289.article |access-date=14 July 2023}}</ref> The former engine manufacturer had offered a new centreline engine in the {{cvt|93|to|102|kN|lb(f)}} thrust class, while the latter was not yet ready to offer its next-generation [[CFM International CFM56|CFM56]] engine,<ref name="FlightGlobalMay2005"/> as Bombardier required a significant upgrade in the event of an engine derivative for the CSeries program.<ref name="FlightGlobal24May2005"/> Both prospective engine suppliers for the CSeries program were uncertain about the aircraft market projections after Bombardier failed to address these concerns, but they left the door open to future discussions of a potential program.<ref name="FlightGlobalMay2005"/> Bombardier then returned to [[Pratt & Whitney]] (P&W) in search of the right engine for the CSeries, although the company had already rejected a [[Pratt & Whitney PW6000|PW6000]] derivative offered by P&W a year earlier, maintaining its original plan to launch the all-new aircraft program only with a new centreline engine as well.<ref name="FlightGlobal24May2005">{{Cite news |date=24 May 2005 |title=Bombardier returns to P&W in search for CSeries engine § |work=Flight Global |url=https://www.flightglobal.com/bombardier-returns-to-pandw-in-search-for-cseries-engine-/60428.article |access-date=14 July 2023}}</ref>

Bombardier announced on 31 January 2006 that market conditions could not justify the launch of the program, and that the company would reorient CSeries project efforts, team and resources to [[Bombardier CRJ700 series|regional jet]] and [[Bombardier Q400|turboprop]] aircraft. A small team of employees were kept to develop the CSeries business plan and were further tasked to include other risk-sharing partners in the program.<ref>{{cite press release |url= http://www.bombardier.com/en/media/newsList/details.282-bombardier-announces-cseries-decision.bombardiercom.html |title= Bombardier Announces CSeries Decision |publisher= Bombardier |date= 31 January 2006 |access-date= 29 June 2016 |archive-date= 20 September 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160920133817/http://www.bombardier.com/en/media/newsList/details.282-bombardier-announces-cseries-decision.bombardiercom.html |url-status= live}}</ref>

Bombardier announced on 31 January 2007 that work on the aircraft would continue, with entry into service planned for 2013.<ref>{{cite press release |url= http://www.bombardier.com/en/media/newsList/details.404-bombardier-updates-market-on-status-of-its-cseries-commercial-aircraft-program.bombardiercom.html |title= Bombardier Updates Market on Status of its CSeries Commercial Aircraft Program |date= 31 January 2007 |publisher= Bombardier |access-date= 29 June 2016 |archive-date= 20 September 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160920142725/http://www.bombardier.com/en/media/newsList/details.404-bombardier-updates-market-on-status-of-its-cseries-commercial-aircraft-program.bombardiercom.html |url-status= live}}</ref> In November 2007, Bombardier finally selected the P&W [[Geared Turbofan]] (GTF), subsequently designated the [[Pratt & Whitney PW1000G|PW1500G]], and already chosen to power the [[Mitsubishi Regional Jet]], to be the exclusive powerplant for the CSeries, rated at {{cvt|23,000|lb(f)|kN|order=flip}}.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Warwick|first1=Graham|title=Bombardier chooses geared turbofan to power CSeries|url=https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/bombardier-chooses-geared-turbofan-to-power-cseries-219523/|access-date=29 June 2016|publisher=[[Flightglobal]]|date=13 November 2007|location=Washington DC|archive-date=22 September 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180922140433/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/bombardier-chooses-geared-turbofan-to-power-cseries-219523/|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Program launch and type redesignation ===
[[File:Bombardier CS100 and CS300 3-view comparison.jpg|thumb|''CSeries'' program was launched at the 2008 [[Farnborough Airshow]] with the ''C110'' and ''C130'' variants, which were redesignated ''CS100'' and ''CS300'' in 2009.]]

Bombardier's Board of Directors authorized offering formal sales proposals of the CSeries to airline customers on 22 February 2008, due to its 20% lower fuel burn and up to 15% better operating costs compared to similarly sized aircraft produced at the time. This interested [[Lufthansa]], [[Qatar Airways]] and [[ILFC]].<ref name="Bomba 20080222">{{cite press release |url= http://www.bombardier.com/en/media/newsList/details.1102-bombardier-grants-authority-to-offer-cseries-the-new-generation-five-abreast-commercial-aircraft.bombardiercom.html |title= Bombardier Grants Authority to Offer CSeries |publisher= Bombardier |date= 22 February 2008 |access-date= 29 June 2016 |archive-date= 20 September 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160920141619/http://www.bombardier.com/en/media/newsList/details.1102-bombardier-grants-authority-to-offer-cseries-the-new-generation-five-abreast-commercial-aircraft.bombardiercom.html |url-status= live}}</ref> In a press conference on the eve of the opening of the Farnborough Airshow on 13 July, Bombardier Aerospace formally launched the CSeries, with a [[letter of interest]] from Lufthansa for 60 aircraft, including 30 options, at a US$46.7{{nbsp}}million list price. The [[Fuel economy in aircraft|aircraft fuel efficiency]] would be {{convert|2|L/100km|mpgUS}} per passenger in a dense seating. Bombardier estimated the market for the 100- to 150-seat segment at 6,300 aircraft over twenty years, representing more than $250 billion in revenue, with the company expected to generate up to half of that.<ref name="AviToday20080717">{{cite news |url= http://www.aviationtoday.com/ran/categories/commercial/Bombardier-Launches-CSeries_24253.html |title= Bombardier Launches CSeries |work= Aviation Today |date= 17 July 2008 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20150118060927/http://www.aviationtoday.com/ran/categories/commercial/Bombardier-Launches-CSeries_24253.html |archive-date= 18 January 2015}}</ref>

Bombardier redesignated the C110 and C130 as ''CS100'' and ''CS300'', respectively in March 2009. The models were offered in standard- and extended-range (ER) variants; and additionally, an extra thrust (XT) variant of the CS300 was also offered.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Kirby|first1=Mary|title=Bombardier makes tweaks to CSeries specs|url=https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/bombardier-makes-tweaks-to-cseries-specs-323716/|publisher=[[Flightglobal]]|date=11 March 2009|location=Philadelphia|archive-date=10 November 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121110211329/http://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/bombardier-makes-tweaks-to-cseries-specs-323716/|url-status=live}}</ref> Bombardier subsequently settled on a single variant, with the ER becoming the new standard.<ref name="cseries_file" />

=== A220 rebranding ===
The aircraft was rebranded A220 as a family name (formerly ''CSeries'') with A220-100/300 (formerly ''CS100/CS300'') as variant name on 10 July 2018, following the [[Airbus A220#Airbus programme acquisition (JV renamed ACLP)|Airbus partnership]] ten days earlier. Financial issues at Bombardier due to the CSeries programme and production delays, stiff competition, and ultimately a dumping petition by Boeing, paved the way for the partnership.<ref name="Leeham18oct2017" />

==== Poor financial situation ====
A [[Airbus A220#CSeries feasibility study|feasibility study]] prior to the programme launch estimated development costs of $2.1 billion for the CSeries in May 2005, shared equally by Bombardier, suppliers and partner governments.<ref name="BombardierMay2005" /> In November 2009, when the first CSeries wing was assembled for [[Airbus A220#Prototype manufacturing|prototype manufacture]], development costs rose to approximately $3.5 billion.<ref name="BloombergNov2009"/> Programme delays during [[Airbus A220#Test preparation & high-density concept|the test preparation]] and [[Airbus A220#Flight testing & program delays|flight test phase]] also resulted in order cancellations, including from a Swedish lessor.<ref>{{cite news |author-last1=Ostrower|author-first1= John |author-first2= Paul |author-last2=Vieira |date=8 January 2015 |title=Jet Maker Bombardier Finds Bigger Proves Far From Better |page=A1 |publisher=Wall Street Journal |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/jet-maker-bombardier-finds-bigger-proves-far-from-better-1420766239 |url-status=live |access-date=5 March 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170511153932/https://www.wsj.com/articles/jet-maker-bombardier-finds-bigger-proves-far-from-better-1420766239 |archive-date=11 May 2017}}</ref> In August 2014, Bombardier changed the programme's management and slashed its workforce.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ho |first1=Solarina |date=19 August 2014 |title=More Bombardier executive reshuffling as CSeries still grounded |url=https://www.reuters.com/article/bombardier-management-idUSL2N0QQ00D20140820 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170928005354/https://www.reuters.com/article/bombardier-management-idUSL2N0QQ00D20140820 |archive-date=28 September 2017 |access-date=30 June 2017 |publisher=Reuters}}</ref>

After reassessing its participation in January 2020, Bombardier exited the A220 programme in February 2020, selling its share to Airbus for $591{{nbsp}}million, when the programme's cost had reached [[US$]]7 billion.<ref>{{cite news|url= https://ici.radio-canada.ca/nouvelle/1526990/bombardier-pdg-alain-bellemare-c-series-vente-airbus-alstom|title= Bombardier "Couldn't Afford" CSeries Alone, Admits CEO Alain Bellemare|date= 20 February 2020|agency= Radio Canada|access-date= 20 February 2020|archive-date= 20 February 2020|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20200220143350/https://ici.radio-canada.ca/nouvelle/1526990/bombardier-pdg-alain-bellemare-c-series-vente-airbus-alstom|url-status= live}}</ref> Airbus thus owned 75% of the programme; the remaining 25% of shares were held by [[Investissement Québec]]. == Design ==
The Airbus A220 family is a five-abreast [[narrow-body aircraft|single-aisle airliner]] developed specifically for the 100- to 150-seat market segment between [[regional airliner]]s and mainline airliners, which includes two models, the {{cvt|35|m|ft|0}} long A220-100 and the larger, {{cvt|38.71|m|ft|0}} long A220-300.<ref name="A220UniqueDesign">{{Cite news |date=10 July 2018 |title=Airbus Introduces the A220-100 and A220-300 |url=https://www.airline-suppliers.com/airbus-introduces-the-a220-100-and-a220-300/ |access-date=28 July 2023 |work=Airline Suppliers}}</ref> The design goal of the unique aircraft was to improve fuel efficiency, as well as operating costs, passenger comfort and range while reducing noise and emissions.<ref name="A220DesignFeatures">{{cite web |url=https://www.airbus.com/en/products-services/commercial-aircraft/passenger-aircraft/a220-family |title= A220 Family - Purpose built for efficiency|website= www.airbus.com|date= 16 June 2021|access-date=5 August 2023}}</ref> These environmental benefits make the A220 family aircraft suitable for urban operations and noise-sensitive airports.<ref name="A220DesignFeatures"/>

===Airframe===
[[File:JetBlue Airbus A220-300 N3145J planform.jpg|thumb|Planform view of an Airbus A220-300 showing exposed wheel wells and moderate wing sweep]]

Commonality between both variants of the A220 family is over 99%. To support higher loads, the A220-300's wing and centre wing box are structurally reinforced, as is the centre [[fuselage]], which is {{cvt|3.4|m|ft}} longer than the -100 variant, and the main [[landing gear]].<ref name="A220 Commonality">{{cite web |url= https://services.airbus.com/content/dam/corporate-topics/publications/fast/Airbus-FAST63.pdf |publisher= Airbus technical magazine |title= A220 Family – the story so far |date= 30 April 2019 |access-date= 4 December 2020 |archive-date= 27 May 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210527114852/https://services.airbus.com/content/dam/corporate-topics/publications/fast/Airbus-FAST63.pdf |url-status= live}}</ref> Extensive use of [[aluminium–lithium alloy|aluminium–lithium]] in the fuselage, and [[carbon composite]] in wings, [[empennage]], rear fuselage section, and [[Nacelle|engine nacelles]] reduces weight and increases corrosion resistance, resulting in better maintainability.<ref name="AirbusPresA220-100" /><ref name="AirbusPresA220-300" /> The overall airframe consists of 70% advanced lightweight materials, comprising 46% composite materials and 24% aluminium–lithium.<ref name="A220_2022file" /> The aircraft features a low drag nose and tailcone design, minimum fuselage [[wetted area]] and optimised wing aerodynamics.<ref name="A220_2022file" />

The nose landing gear is common for both variants, while the -300 main landing gear is slightly reinforced. The -100 has three pairs of disc brakes, the -300 one more.<ref name="A220 Commonality" />

=== Cabin ===
[[File:JetBlue A220 - Interior (cabin).jpg|thumb|Five-abreast cabin and {{cvt|18.5|in|cm}} wide economy seats]]

The five-abreast cabin [[Cross section (geometry)|cross section]] has {{cvt|18.5|in|cm|1|order=flip}} wide economy seats, {{cvt|19|in|cm|1|order=flip}} wide middle seats, and a {{cvt|20|in|cm|1|order=flip}} wide aisle for fast turnarounds of 20{{nbsp}}minutes. The rotating overhead bins offer {{cvt|70|L|cuft}} of storage per passenger to allow one carry-on bag per passenger. Each row has power cables, so all seats are equipped with charging capabilities.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Introducing Air Canada's A220 |url=https://www.aircanada.com/ca/en/aco/home/fly/onboard/fleet/a220.html |access-date=2025-11-07 |website=www.aircanada.com |language=en-ca}}</ref> Lavatories have improved accessibility for passengers with reduced mobility.<ref name="A220_2022file" /> Two ''flex zones'' allow modular cabin elements such as stowage areas and partitions to be customised.<ref name="AirbusPresA220-100" /><ref name="AirbusPresA220-300" /> The cabin is lighted naturally through {{cvt|11x16|in|cm|order=flip}} windows (larger than those on the A320<ref>{{Cite web |last=Welt |first=Flying |date=2023-07-24 |title=Airbus A220: Redefining the Future of Regional Aviation |url=https://www.flyingwelt.com/2023/07/airbus-a220-redefining-the-future-of-regional-aviation/ |access-date=2023-11-21 |website=Flying Welt |language=en-US}}</ref>) at every seat row and artificially by customisable colour [[Light-emitting diode|LED]]s. The aircraft offers overhead video display, wireless content distribution and [[Ku band]] connectivity, and can be equipped with [[In-flight entertainment|in-flight-entertainment]].<ref name="A220_2022file" /> The onboard environment, entertainment offerings and [[mood lighting]] are controlled via an integrated cabin management system.<ref name="AirbusPresA220-100" /><ref name="AirbusPresA220-300" />

It has a {{cvt|4|in|cm|order=flip}} higher ceiling as well as 20% larger luggage bins than other aircraft in its class.{{vague|reason=which other aircraft in its class?|date=February 2023}} The seat is {{cvt|2.5|cm|in|1}} wider than the Airbus A320 and {{cvt|5.0|cm|in}} wider than the Boeing 737.<ref name="A220 Commonality" />  The new ''A220 Airspace XL'' bins would offer up to 19 additional passenger bags on the A220-300 and accommodate longer and heavier payload items thanks to the four-frame design.<ref name="A220Airspace">{{cite press release |title=A220 steps into the Airspace Family with new cabin design features |url=https://aircraft.airbus.com/en/newsroom/news/2023-06-a220-steps-into-the-airspace-family-with-new-cabin-design-features |date=6 June 2023 |publisher=Airbus}}</ref> The bins would also reduce maintenance and the effort for cabin crew to close the bin doors, resulting in an overall shorter [[turnaround time]] and about {{convert|300|lb|kg|order=flip|adj=on}} lighter cabin structure.<ref name="A220Airspace" /> To complement the Airspace XL bins, an improved Passenger Service Unit (PSU) was developed in line with the Airspace design.<ref name="AirSpace" />

=== Cockpit ===
[[File:AirBaltic Bombardier CS300 maintenance (33221388195).jpg|thumb|Cockpit with [[side-stick]] controller]]

The cockpit features the [[Rockwell Collins]] Pro Line Fusion avionics suite, which incorporates five {{cvt|15.1|in|cm|order=flip}} displays along with comprehensive navigation, communications, surveillance, [[engine-indicating and crew-alerting system]] (EICAS), electronic checklist, aircraft maintenance systems,<ref>{{cite press release |title= Bombardier Selects Rockwell Collins Pro Line Fusion(TM) for CSeries |url= http://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20080713005026/en/Bombardier-Selects-Rockwell-Collins-Pro-Line-Fusion |date= 13 July 2008 |publisher= Rockwell Collins |access-date= 29 June 2016 |archive-date= 4 March 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160304195639/http://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20080713005026/en/Bombardier-Selects-Rockwell-Collins-Pro-Line-Fusion |url-status= live}}</ref> and can be equipped with [[head-up display]]s.<ref name="A220 Commonality" /> Other elements of the avionics and other subsystems include [[Parker Hannifin]]'s flight control, fuel and hydraulics systems; [[Liebherr]] Aerospace's air management system; and [[United Technologies Corporation]]'s air data system, flap and slat actuation systems.<ref name="flight1June2009" /> The cockpit includes a dual [[flight management system]], multi-scan weather radar, [[fly-by-wire]] flight controls with full envelope protection & speed stabilisation, Cat IIIa Autoland, and [[side-stick]] controllers. The cockpit layout is common to the -100 and the -300 variants, enabling pilots to fly either variant with the same [[type rating]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.airbus.com/en/products-services/commercial-aircraft/cockpits |title=Commercial aircraft. Cockpits|website=www.airbus.com|date=16 June 2021 |access-date=2023-02-07}}</ref>

===Engine===
[[File:Bombardier CS100 (22836277953).jpg|thumb|PW1500G [[geared turbofan]] mounted under the wing]]

The A220 is powered by two [[Pratt & Whitney PW1000G|Pratt & Whitney PW1500G]] underwing turbofans.<ref name="A220_2022file" /> Its [[geared turbofan]] (GTF) architecture and advanced engine core improves efficiency and reduces the stage and parts count.<ref name="PW1500Gpresskit" /> The PW1500G has a 20 dB margin to Chapter IV [[Aircraft noise|noise]] limits, and high-efficiency components and advanced [[combustor]] technologies reduce {{CO2}} and [[NOx]] emissions.<ref name="PW1500Gpresskit">{{cite web |url= https://filecache.mediaroom.com/mr5mr_prattwhitney/177481/download/PW1500G.S16310.K.05.17.pdf |title= PurePower PW1500G Engine |publisher= Pratt & Whitney}}</ref> It was certified in February 2013, the first variant in the PW1000G range.<ref name="PW1500Gpresskit" /> At that time, the PW1500G was the turbofan engine with the highest [[bypass ratio]] (BPR) of 12:1,<ref name="PW1500Gpresskit" /> only slightly lower than the 12.5:1 BPR of the later released PW1100G powering the [[A320neo family]].<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.mtu.de/engines/commercial-aircraft-engines/narrowbody-and-regional-jets/pw1000g/ |title= PW1000G |publisher= [[MTU Aero Engines|MTU]] |access-date= 2016-05-31 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180818154807/https://www.mtu.de/engines/commercial-aircraft-engines/narrowbody-and-regional-jets/pw1000g/ |archive-date= 2018-08-18 |url-status= dead}}</ref> Each engine can produce {{cvt|84.5|to|104|kN|lb(f)}} of thrust [[flat rated]] at [[International Standard Atmosphere|ISA]] +15 °C.<ref name="PW1500Gpresskit" />
The PW1500G was designed to reach 12% better fuel economy than previous generation engines.<ref>{{cite news |url= https://www.nytimes.com/2008/07/14/business/worldbusiness/14air.html |title= A New Bombardier Jet Draws Only Tepid Demand |newspaper= The New York Times |date= 14 July 2008}}</ref><!-- consistent with "Double-digit fuel burn reduction"-->

=== Efficiency ===
The A220 manufacturer states that the structural technology, aerodynamic design, ultra-high bypass GTF engine, and [[state-of-the-art]] flight control and systems together can save [[Fuel economy in aircraft|fuel burn per seat]], {{CO2}} and [[NOx]] emissions,<ref name="AirbusPresA220-100" /><ref name="AirbusPresA220-300" /> as well as provide a reduction in [[maintenance costs]] and [[operating cost]] per seat, plus a reduced noise footprint with a 18 EPNdB margin to [[Aircraft noise pollution#Regulation|chapter 4]] noise limits.<ref name="A220_2022file" /> Around two thirds of the overall fuel efficiency are attributed to the GTF engines, and one third to lightweight structures, state-of-the-art aerodynamics and systems.<ref name="A220 Commonality" />

=== Decarbonisation ===
The A220 family plays a key role in Airbus's commitment to its [[decarbonisation]] targets. The fuel-efficient aircraft can already fly with a blend of up to 50% [[Sustainable Aviation Fuel]] (SAF) and, like all other Airbus commercial aircraft, will be certified for 100% SAF capability by 2030.<ref name="5yrsA220"/> On 25 August 2025, [[Air France]] took delivery of its 46th A220-300 with a ferry flight from Airbus Canada, which for the first time used a fuel blend containing 50% SAF, certified directly by Airbus.<ref>{{Cite news |date=26 August 2025 |title=Air France-KLM takes delivery of 46th A220 on a landmark ferry flight with Airbus using 50% sustainable aviation fuel |url=https://www.airfranceklm.com/en/newsroom/air-france-klm-takes-delivery-46th-a220-landmark-ferry-flight-airbus-using-50-sustainable |access-date=30 August 2025 |work=Air France-KLM Group}}</ref>

=== Engine issues ===

==== Noise ====
[[File:JetBlue Airbus A220 N3194J take off Boston July 2025.webm|thumb|right|The PW1500G's whale-like noise can be heard at the beginning of this video of a [[JetBlue]] A220-300 taking off from [[Logan International Airport|Boston]].]]

The engines can emit a loud howl for a few seconds during throttle movements at low power settings. This distinctive howl was likened to the mating call of an [[orca]], and led to noise complaints from residents near Zurich Airport when [[Swiss International Air Lines]] started operating the A220.<ref>{{cite web |date=November 6, 2018 |title=Airbus A220 'Whisperjet' is too loud, according to Zurich residents |url=https://www.smh.com.au/traveller/inspiration/airbus-a220-whisperjet-is-too-loud-according-to-zurich-residents-20181106-h17jqc.html |access-date=July 21, 2025 |work=The Sydney Morning Herald Traveller}}</ref> A Pratt and Whitney official says that the engine noise is caused by a "low power transient combustor tone" which generally occurs on approach when the engine is at low or idle power. Under those conditions, the flame front inside the combustor causes pressure perturbations that interact with the walls of the combustor to create the whale sound. The noise has no repercussions on the operation of the engine.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Petchenik |first=Ian |date=2020-12-04 |title=AvTalk Episode 99: Solving the mystery of the whale song |url=https://www.flightradar24.com/blog/avtalk-podcast/avtalk-episode-99-solving-the-mystery-of-the-whale-song/ |access-date=2025-06-03 |website=Flightradar24 Blog |language=en-US}}</ref>

==== Reliability ====
Since the PW1500G mount generates less strain on the [[Rotor (turbine)|turbine rotor]] assembly than the A320neo's PW1100G, it does not suffer from start-up and [[Bearing (mechanical)|bearing]] problems but still from premature [[combustor]] degradation.<ref name="Flight14Jul2017" /> An updated combustor liner with a 6,000–8,000{{nbsp}}hour limit has been developed and a third generation for 2018 will raise it to 20,000{{nbsp}}hours in benign environments.<ref name="Flight14Jul2017" />

After three inflight engine failures in 2019, [[Transport Canada]] issued an [[emergency airworthiness directive]] (EAD) limiting the power to 94% of N1 (Low Pressure Spool rotational speed) above {{cvt|29,000|ft}}, disengaging the [[autothrottle]] for the climb over this altitude before engaging it again in cruise.<ref>{{cite news |author-first1=David |author-last1=Kaminski-Morrow |date=28 Oct 2019 |title=A220 operators told to limit engine thrust at high altitude |url=https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/a220-operators-told-to-limit-engine-thrust-at-high-a-461843/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191030232730/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/a220-operators-told-to-limit-engine-thrust-at-high-a-461843/ |archive-date=30 October 2019 |access-date=30 October 2019 |work=Flightglobal}}</ref>

In June 2026<!--officials from both companies provided the details at a media briefing on June 24-->, Airbus and Pratt & Whitney said the A220's engine issues have largely been resolved and expected that no A220 aircraft to remain grounded due to a lack of spare engines by the end of 2026. Only 2-3% of the grounded A220s are due to the engine problems at the time.<ref name=LNA07072026>{{cite news |last1=Hamilton |first1=Scott |title=A220 engine problems nearly over, say Airbus and Pratt & Whitney |url=https://leehamnews.com/2026/07/07/a220-engine-problems-nearly-over-say-airbus-and-pratt-whitney/ |access-date=17 October 2026 |work=Leeham News |date=7 July 2026}}</ref>

=== Maintenance ===
The A check originally took 5{{nbsp}}hours and has since been reduced to less than 3{{nbsp}}hours, fitting within an 8-hour work shift. It was scheduled after 850 flight hours,<ref name=Flight14Jul2017/> and this threshold has been increased to 1,000 flight hours.<ref name="A220_FAF_last" /> The C check is scheduled after 8,500{{nbsp}}hours – translating to about 3.5 years of operation,<ref name=Flight14Jul2017/> and the interval could increase to 10,000{{nbsp}}hours.<ref name=Flight14Jul2017>{{cite news |url= https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/analysis-how-has-the-cseries-performed-in-service-439012/ |author-first1= Michael |author-last1=Gubisch |work= Flightglobal |title= How has the CSeries performed in service? |date= 14 July 2017 |access-date= 17 July 2017 |archive-date= 30 November 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251130000619/https://www.flightglobal.com/analysis/analysis-how-has-the-cseries-performed-in-service/124690.article |url-status= live}}</ref>

==Variants==
There are two main variants of the five-abreast A220 family: the {{cvt|35|m|ft|0}} long A220-100 including the ACJ TwoTwenty [[Airbus Corporate Jets|corporate jet]] version, and the {{cvt|3.7|m|ft|0}} longer A220-300. Their over 99% [[commonality]] allows a common [[spare part]] inventory, reducing investment and maintenance costs.<ref name="A220 Commonality" />

The A220-100 ([[List of ICAO aircraft type designators|ICAO code]]: BCS1) is the shorter variant of the A220 family at {{cvt|35|m|ft|0}} in length that can fly between 100 and 135 passengers over a distance of {{Cvt|6667|km|nmi|disp=output only}} ({{Cvt|6667|km|km|disp=output only}}; {{Cvt|6667|km|mi|disp=output only}}).<ref name="AirbusPresA220-100">{{Cite web |date=2021-10-07 |title=A220-100 {{!}} A220 {{!}} Aircraft {{!}} Airbus Aircraft |url=https://aircraft.airbus.com/en/aircraft/a220/a220-100 |access-date=2022-08-01 |website=aircraft.airbus.com |language=en}}</ref> The former ''CS100'' made its maiden flight on 16 September 2013 and was first delivered to the launch operator Swiss Global Air Lines on 29 June 2016. The type entered service on 15 July 2016 with a revenue flight between Zurich and Paris. The A220-100 has a takeoff distance of {{cvt|4800|ft|m|order=flip}} and a landing distance of {{cvt|4550|ft|m|order=flip}} and is also certified for steep approaches by Transport Canada and EASA,<ref name=SteepApproachCert/> making it one of the largest aircraft that can land at [[London City Airport]] (LCY) and connect it non-stop to [[New York City]] [[John F. Kennedy International Airport]] (JFK).<ref name="ainonline29March2017">{{Cite news |last=Polek |first=Gregory |date=29 March 2017 |title=Embraer E195-E2 Narrowbody Airliner Takes Flight |work=AIN Online |url=https://www.ainonline.com/aviation-news/air-transport/2017-03-29/embraer-e195-e2-narrowbody-airliner-takes-flight |access-date=15 October 2023}}</ref> The model marketing designation is the BD-500-1A10 for aircraft from serial number 50011,<ref name="faatcds">{{cite web |url= https://rgl.faa.gov/Regulatory_and_Guidance_Library/rgMakeModel.nsf/0/8f2757758f3b2afb8625833100722e1c/$FILE/T00008NY_Rev_4.pdf |publisher= Federal Aviation Administration |title= Type Certificate Data Sheet T0008NY for the CSALP BD-500 |date= 18 October 2018 |access-date= 20 November 2018 |archive-date= 21 November 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20181121022041/https://rgl.faa.gov/Regulatory_and_Guidance_Library/rgMakeModel.nsf/0/8f2757758f3b2afb8625833100722e1c/$FILE/T00008NY_Rev_4.pdf |url-status= dead}}</ref> including the first aircraft delivered to [[Swiss International Air Lines|Swiss]] (MSN-50010).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Civil Database |url=https://www.scramble.nl/database/civil#results |access-date=23 November 2024 |website=Scramble civil aircraft database}}</ref>

The A220-100, the smallest jetliner within the Airbus product line,<ref name="AirbusPresA220-100" /> competes with largest members of the four-abreast [[Embraer E-Jet E2 family]], the [[Embraer E195-E2|E195-E2]] and [[Embraer E190-E2|E190-E2]], replacing the previous generation [[E-195]], [[E190]], as well as the five/six-abreast [[Boeing 717]], [[737-600]], [[Airbus A318]] and ageing models: [[McDonnell Douglas DC-9]]/[[McDonnell Douglas MD-80#MD-87|MD-87]], [[Fokker 100]], [[BAe-146]], and [[Boeing 737-500]]. The A220-100 is well ahead of the two E-Jet E2 variants in terms of range and payload, but the latter has a lower base price due to its more conservative design and correspondingly cheaper production costs.<ref name="ainonline29March2017" /> The unit price of an A220-100 is estimated at $81{{nbsp}}million, while an E-190 E2 and E-195 E2 are priced at $61{{nbsp}}million and $69{{nbsp}}million, respectively.<ref name="Pilotpass31May2023">{{Cite web |last=Walsh |first=Sean |date=31 May 2023 |title=How Much Does an Airbus Plane Cost? |url=https://pilotpassion.com/how-much-does-an-airbus-plane-cost/ |access-date=22 October 2023}}</ref><ref name="Leeham26Feb2018">{{Cite news |last=Hamilton |first=Scott |date=26 February 2018 |title=Pontifications: OEMs hike list prices |work=Leeham News |url=https://leehamnews.com/2018/02/26/pontifications-oems-hike-list-prices/ |access-date=22 October 2023}}</ref> {{As of|2026|10}}, there are 75 A220-100s in revenue service with five operators, where [[Delta Air Lines|Delta]] is the largest operator with 45 aircraft in its fleet.<ref name="Airbus_O&D" />

===A220-300===
[[File:Delta Airbus A220-300 N333DU departing Boston June 2025.jpg|thumb|The A220-300 is the larger variant with a {{cvt|38.71|m|ft|0}} long fuselage or {{cvt|3.7|m|ft|0}} longer than A220-100.|alt=The A220-300 is the larger variant with a 3.7 m (12 ft) longer fuselage than A220-100.]]

The A220-300 ([[List of ICAO aircraft type designators|ICAO code]]: BCS3) is the larger variant with a {{cvt|38.71|m|ft|0}} long fuselage or {{cvt|3.7|m|ft|0}} longer than A220-100 and can carry between 120 and 160 passengers over a distance of {{cvt|{{#expr:3400+200}}|nmi}}.<ref name=AirbusPresA220-300>{{Cite web |date=2021-10-07 |title=A220-300 {{!}} A220 {{!}} Aircraft {{!}} Airbus Aircraft |url=https://aircraft.airbus.com/en/aircraft/a220/a220-300 |access-date=2022-08-01 |website=aircraft.airbus.com |language=en}}</ref> The former ''CS300'' had its maiden flight on 27 February 2015, and the first delivery to airBaltic, the type launch operator, in November 2016. The type entered service on 14 December with a revenue flight from Riga to Amsterdam in a 145 seat two-class configuration. In several [[Airbus A220#Performance improvements|performance improvements]], the MTOW and thus the permissible tank content were increased, where Delta received the first improved aircraft on 18 June 2019.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Kaminski-Morrow |first=David |date=18 June 2019 |title=PARIS: Delta to take higher-weight A220 |work=FlightGlobal |url=https://www.flightglobal.com/fleets/paris-delta-to-take-higher-weight-a220/133211.article |access-date=9 July 2023}}</ref> Airbus offered a further {{cvt|1|t|lb}} increase to the MTOW of the A220-300, to {{cvt|70.9|t|lb}} in March 2021, providing another {{cvt|200|nmi}} of additional range to {{cvt|3550|nmi}}. On long routes the payload will be increased by about {{cvt|900|kg|lb}}. The model marketing designation is the BD-500-1A11 for aircraft from serial number 55003.<ref name="faatcds" />

The A220-300 complements the [[A319neo]] in the Airbus fleet and competes with the [[Boeing 737 MAX|Boeing 737 MAX 7]] and, to some extent, with the [[Embraer E195-E2]], replacing previous generation airliners, smaller variants of the [[Boeing 737 Next Generation|737 Next Gen]]/[[Boeing 737 Classic|737 Classic]] and [[McDonnell Douglas MD-90]]/[[McDonnell Douglas MD-80|MD-80 series]]. The A220-300 was designed to be {{cvt|6|t|lb}} lighter than the A319neo and nearly {{cvt|8|t|lb}} lighter than the 737 MAX 7, giving it better operating costs of up to 12%.<ref name="300Efficiency"/> Furthermore, the unit price of an A220-300 is estimated at just $91.5{{nbsp}}million, while an A319neo is priced at $101.5{{nbsp}}million.<ref name="Pilotpass31May2023" /><ref name="Leeham26Feb2018" /> These cost advantages and other aspects contribute to the A220-300 outselling the A319neo as well as the 737-7.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kamoun |first=Skander |date=28 September 2020 |title=Infographic – Will the Airbus A220 be the narrow-body aircraft of tomorrow? |url=https://blog.flight-report.com/infographic-airbus-a220-narrow-body-aircraft-tomorrow/ |access-date=12 April 2024 |website=Flight-Report}}</ref><ref name="Boeing_O-D">{{cite web |date=30 June 2025 |title=Boeing Orders and Deliveries (737) |url=https://www.boeing.com/commercial/#/orders-deliveries |access-date=8 July 2025 |publisher=Boeing}}</ref> {{As of|2026|10}}, there are 480 A220-300s in commercial service with 23 operators, where [[JetBlue]] is the largest operator with 70 aircraft in its fleet.<ref name="Airbus_O&D" />

===ACJ TwoTwenty===
{{See also|Airbus Corporate Jets#ACJ TwoTwenty}}Since 2020, the Airbus A220 has also been available as a [[business jet]] under the name ACJ TwoTwenty, which is a variant of the A220-100 with a range of {{cvt|5650|nmi|mi km}} and customisable cabin space of {{cvt|73|sqm}} for 18 passengers. To increase its range, the type is offered with up to five removable auxiliary centre [[fuel tank]]s.<ref>{{cite web |date=6 September 2021 |title=ACJ TwoTwenty {{!}} Airbus Corporate Jets |url=https://www.acj.airbus.com/en/exclusive-aircraft/acj-twotwenty |access-date=9 July 2023 |website=www.acj.airbus.com}}</ref> The ACJ TwoTwenty made its first flight on 14 December 2021, and was to be outfitted with a VIP cabin in [[Indianapolis]], before its first delivery to [[Comlux]] expected in 2023.<ref name="AvWebOct2021">{{cite news |last1=O'Connor |first1=Kate |title=ACJ TwoTwenty On Schedule For 2023 Debut |url=https://www.avweb.com/aviation-news/business-aviation-news/acj-twotwenty-on-schedule-for-2023/ |access-date=14 October 2021 |work=AVweb |date=13 October 2021}}</ref>

==Accidents and incidents==
The A220 family has recorded one engine-related accident with one fatality due to smoke on board, and one hull loss following a ground fire, {{as of|2026|03|lc=yes}}.<ref>{{Cite web |date=December 2025 |title=Safety Database of the Airbus A220 |url=https://asn.flightsafety.org/asndb/type/_A220 |website=[[Aviation Safety Network]]}}</ref>

=== Accidents ===
* On 23 December 2024, a [[SWISS International Air Lines]] A220-300 operating as [[Swiss International Air Lines Flight 1885|Flight 1885]] from [[Henri Coanda International Airport]] to [[Zurich Airport]], diverted to [[Graz Airport]] after smoke developed in the cabin and cockpit due to an engine problem, while in cruise flight at FL400. All 79 people on board were evacuated via emergency slides, and the five crew members plus twelve passengers received medical treatment, while an incapacitated cabin crew member was rushed to hospital by helicopter, but died a week later on 30 December.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ranter |first=Harro |title=Accident Airbus A220-300 HB-JCD, Monday 23 December 2024 |url=https://asn.flightsafety.org/wikibase/468093 |access-date=2024-12-30 |website=asn.flightsafety.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Kaminski-Morrow |first=David |date=31 December 2024 |title=Swiss cabin crew member dies after A220's engine-related diversion |url=https://www.flightglobal.com/safety/swiss-cabin-crew-member-dies-after-a220s-engine-related-diversion/161251.article |access-date=4 January 2025 |work=[[FlightGlobal]]}}</ref>
* On 14 June 2025, an [[airBaltic]] Airbus A220-300 was undergoing an [[auxiliary power unit]] ground-run during scheduled maintenance when a fire ignited in the centre section of the aircraft. The fire was reportedly caused by an ozone filter and resulted in significant thermal damage to the fuselage and wing root section, but no injuries. In December 2025, Airbus Engineering concluded that the aircraft was uneconomical to repair. The aircraft was then written off, marking the first hull loss of an A220 family aircraft.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Peters|first=Luke|date=2026-03-17|title=First Airbus A220 hull loss confirmed after fire destroys airBaltic jet|url=https://aerospaceglobalnews.com/news/airbus-a220-first-hull-loss-airbaltic/|access-date=2026-03-18|website=AGN|language=en-en}}</ref>

=== Incidents ===
* After three [[Turbine engine failure|inflight shutdown]]s due to [[Pratt & Whitney PW1000G#PW1500G failures|PW1500G engine failure]] in July, September, and October 2019, [[Swiss International Air Lines]] temporarily withdrew its fleet for inspection.<ref>{{cite news|title=Third Swiss A220 failure spurs urgent engine checks|url=https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/third-swiss-a220-failure-spurs-urgent-engine-checks-461504/|date=October 15, 2019|author-first1=David |author-last1=Kaminiski-Morrow|work=FlightGlobal|access-date=6 November 2019|archive-date=22 October 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191022104119/https://www.flightglobal.com/news/articles/third-swiss-a220-failure-spurs-urgent-engine-checks-461504/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.industryweek.com/technology-and-iiot/article/22028404/swiss-grounds-airbus-a220-planes-after-finding-engine-fault|title=Swiss Grounds Airbus A220 Planes After Finding Engine Fault|website=Industry Week|date=Oct 15, 2019|access-date=10 April 2021|archive-date=10 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210410203419/https://www.industryweek.com/technology-and-iiot/article/22028404/swiss-grounds-airbus-a220-planes-after-finding-engine-fault|url-status=live}}</ref>

* On 4 January 2025, an [[Air Canada]] A220-300 operating as AC609 from [[Halifax Stanfield International Airport]] to [[Toronto-Pearson International Airport]] suffered a pressurization issue during the climb. Unable to adjust the cabin altitude in manual control, the crew decided to return to base (RTB). After replacing the aft cargo vent flap idler bearing, which had sheared off and caused the vent to open, the aircraft was returned to service.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://asn.flightsafety.org/wikibase/469871 |title=Loss of pressurization Incident Airbus A220-300 C-GUPG, Saturday 4 January 2025}}</ref>

== Aircraft on display ==
* The third flight test vehicle or FTV3 (A220-100) with around 1,400 flight hours was officially donated on 17 October 2018 at [[MET – Montreal Metropolitan Airport|St-Hubert airport]] to Quebec’s [[École nationale d'aérotechnique|École Nationale d’Aérotechnique]] (ÉNA), the Canadian province’s sole provider of technical training for aerospace workers, a school affiliated with cégep Édouard-Montpetit.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Van Leeuven |first=Marcel |date=17 October 2018 |title=CSeries Aircraft Lands at École nationale d'aérotechnique to Start New Training Mission |url=https://aviationnews.eu/news/2018/10/c-series-aircraft-lands-at-ecole-nationale-daerotechnique-to-start-new-training-mission/ |access-date=24 August 2024 |work=[[Aviation News]]}}</ref>
* The first flight test vehicle or FTV1 (A220-100) with around 760 flight hours was converted into an ''A220 full-size mock-up'' on 28 May 2021, at the Airspace Customer Showroom (ACS) located in [[Toulouse]], France. The mock-up will be used by customers who have already selected the A220 and for Airbus to design new cabin layouts. Airlines that are in the final stages of configuring their aircraft will be able to test their lighting and seat selection on the mock-up before their aircraft is delivered.<ref>{{Cite news |date=28 May 2021 |title=Airbus reveals its new A220 full size cabin display |work=[[Airbus]] |url=https://www.airbus.com/en/newsroom/news/2021-05-airbus-reveals-its-new-a220-full-size-cabin-display |access-date=22 December 2023}}</ref>
* The second and seventh flight test vehicles FTV2 (A220-100) and FTV7 (A220-300) respectively were repatriated in December 2023 from [[Wichita, Kansas|Wichita]], [[Kansas]] (USA) to the main facility in Mirabel, Quebec, where both became part of the ''A220 Flight and Integration Tests Center'', which began operations on 1 January 2024.<ref name="A220_FAF_last"/> It is the second Airbus flight test center, consisting of the two aforementioned test aircraft and aircraft test beds, and is intended to ensure continuous improvement of the A220 family aircraft, in particular by supporting the development of sustainable aviation fuels and studies on the recycling of aviation materials through the partnerships between Airbus, SMEs, research centers and universities.<ref>{{Cite news |date=23 July 2024 |title=Airbus continues to invest in the A220 and extends its partnership with the Government of Quebec |url=https://www.marketwatch.com/press-release/airbus-continues-to-invest-in-the-a220-and-extends-its-partnership-with-the-government-of-quebec-2c747af1 |access-date=3 August 2024 |work=Market Watch}}</ref>
